temptingClaims: The light-quantum paper was written to answer the “ultraviolet catastrophe”.
whyTempting: Textbooks introduce light quanta with that phrase, and § 1 of the paper does show that the classical theory gives an infinite energy.
whereItIsTrue: § 1 shows exactly the difficulty the phrase later named: the classical equilibrium between resonators and radiation gives a radiation energy that grows without limit as higher frequencies are included.

whatIsTrue.r0: The phrase does not occur in the paper. § 1 shows the classical infinity as one difficulty, and the paper's argument for light quanta rests on something else, the entropy of radiation of low density.
whatIsTrue.r1: § 1, “On a difficulty concerning the theory of black radiation”, finds that the condition of dynamic equilibrium derived classically not only fails to agree with experience, but also means there can be no talk of a definite distribution of energy between ether and matter: the wider the range of resonator frequencies, the larger the radiation energy of the space, and in the limit it is infinite (p. 136). The paper then leaves that result and argues for quanta from the Wien region: the entropy of dilute monochromatic radiation depends on volume as that of a gas of independent quanta does (§§ 4–6, p. 143). LQ-02 shows the § 1 difficulty: widening the cutoff tenfold multiplies the classical energy by a thousand, and the lab refuses to report a total.
whatIsTrue.r2:
(1) Classical equilibrium gives each resonator the mean energy \( rac{R}{N}T\), and the radiation density \(ho_
u =  rac{R}{N} rac{8\pi
u^2}{L^3}T\) (p. 136). (2) The energy up to a cutoff \(
u_c\) is the integral of \(ho_
u\), in proportion to \(
u_c^3\). (3) A tenfold cutoff gives a thousandfold energy, and with no cutoff the integral is infinite, as the paper writes: \(\int_0^\infty ho_
u\,d
u = \infty\). (4) The paper's quanta come from a different place: §§ 4–6 compare the entropy of dilute radiation with that of a gas. (5) So § 1 is a difficulty the paper records, not the argument it builds its proposal on.
whatIsTrue.r3: The phrase “ultraviolet catastrophe” is a later coinage, and what Ehrenfest actually wrote is narrower than the English catchphrase. Section IV of his 1911 paper, on p. 92, is headed “Die Vermeidung der Rayleigh-Jeans-Katastrophe im Ultravioletten”: the catastrophe he names belongs to the Rayleigh-Jeans formula in the ultraviolet, not to classical physics at large, and the same page calls his two conditions the Rotforderung and the Violettforderung. The short English form came later. Read against the 1905 paper, the point stands twice over: the phrase is six years after it, and the difficulty it names is one Einstein treats in § 1 and does not build his argument on.
